claims.text: Adding approximately 10–30% Ni to Pt nanoparticles forms isolated Pt ensembles embedded in a Ni-rich matrix.
Ni incorporation produces surface strain in the Pt–Ni nanoparticles.
Ni incorporation shifts the Pt d-band center or otherwise measurably shifts Pt electronic states.
The shifted Pt d-band center changes the adsorption energies of ethanol and its oxidation intermediates.
The adsorption-energy changes promote a selective multi-electron, multi-proton ethanol-oxidation pathway.
Ni-induced electronic modification facilitates proton desorption.
Ni-induced electronic modification mitigates carbonaceous poisoning of the catalyst.
Suppressing poisoning and optimizing intermediate binding increases ethanol-oxidation activity relative to pure Pt nanoparticles.
Suppressing poisoning and optimizing intermediate binding improves product selectivity relative to pure Pt nanoparticles.
The electronic modifications improve catalyst durability and sustain catalytic performance relative to pure Pt nanoparticles.
Pt–Ni composition has an optimum for ethanol-oxidation activity and selectivity within the tested 10–30% Ni range.
The optimal Pt–Ni composition is likely to contain approximately 20% Ni.
Catalytic performance enhancements will correlate with a measurable shift in Pt electronic states.
The proposed mechanism applies to ethanol oxidation in alkaline media at 25–70 °C.
At high temperatures or in acidic media, alternative kinetic or stability effects may supersede the proposed mechanism.
Catalysis theory supports Ni-mediated tuning of the Pt d-band structure.

contradictions.description: The proposed alloys contain only 10–30% Ni and are therefore compositionally Pt-rich, yet the mediator is described as isolated Pt ensembles embedded in a Ni-rich matrix. This requires an unstated and unverified surface-segregation or reconstruction mechanism.
